faq.q: Why is proteinuria the key diagnostic clue?

faq.a: Yes, up to 30 % remit spontaneously, especially if PLA2R titres fall.
faq.q: Can membranous nephropathy resolve without immunosuppression?

faq.a: Steroids alone are ineffective; they are used only as part of combination regimens with calcineurin inhibitors.

exam: How does the histologic stage of MN influence prognosis? — Higher stage (III‑IV) correlates with more chronic changes and lower likelihood of remission.
Why are ACE‑I/ARB preferred as first‑line therapy in MN? — They reduce intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria without major immunosuppression.
A patient with MN develops a deep vein thrombosis; what anticoagulation strategy is appropriate? — Initiate low‑molecular‑weight heparin unless contraindicated, then transition to oral anticoagulant.
What secondary causes are most common in East African hospitals and how do you screen for them? — HIV, hepatitis B, malaria, schistosomiasis; order serology, rapid tests, and malaria smear.
When is a kidney biopsy essential in suspected MN? — When secondary causes are excluded, proteinuria persists despite ACE‑I/ARB, or rapid renal decline occurs.
Explain why high‑dose steroids alone are avoided in MN. — They provide little benefit and increase infection risk, especially in HIV‑prevalent settings.
What clinical feature distinguishes MN from minimal change disease in adults? — MN often has persistent proteinuria despite steroids and may show anti‑PLA2R antibodies.
ai.title: Membranous Nephropathy
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: An immune-mediated cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults, characterised by subepithelial immune deposits on the glomerular basement membrane. Diagnosis relies on proteinuria, serology and kidney biopsy; management targets the underlying cause and proteinuria.

b: Nephrotic syndrome: proteinuria ≥3.5 g/24 h, hypoalbuminaemia <30 g/L, oedema, hyperlipidaemia.
Primary (autoantibody PLA2R) vs secondary (infections, drugs, systemic disease).
sections.p: Membranous nephropathy (MN) is the commonest cause of adult nephrotic syndrome in many low‑resource settings. It results from immune complex deposition on the outer aspect of the glomerular basement membrane, leading to thickened capillary walls and selective loss of albumin.

b: Stage I: granular IgG along capillary loops; Stage II: spike formation; Stage III: thickened membrane; Stage IV: sclerosis.
Common secondary triggers in East Africa: malaria, hepatitis B, HIV, schistosomiasis, herbal nephrotoxins.
sections.p: The disease is staged histologically (stage I–IV) by the appearance of subepithelial deposits and basement‑membrane reaction. In low‑resource hospitals, clinical suspicion often precedes biopsy.

b: Venous thromboembolism risk rises when serum albumin <20 g/L.
Rapid rise in serum creatinine (>30 % in 2 weeks) signals impending renal failure.
sections.p: Patients present with painless oedema, often periorbital in the morning, and frothy urine. Complications include thromboembolic events, acute kidney injury, and progression to end‑stage renal disease.

t.b: Quantifies proteinuria; >3.5 g/24 h confirms nephrotic range.
Assesses nephrotic syndrome severity and renal function.
Distinguishes primary from secondary MN; positive supports primary disease.

t.a: Hepatitis B surface antigen, HIV test, malaria smear
t.b: Screens for common secondary causes in the region.
Confirms diagnosis, stages disease, and excludes other glomerulopathies.
Detects chronic changes, rules out obstruction.

b: If secondary cause identified – treat infection (e.g., antiretroviral for HIV, antimalarial, antiviral for hepatitis B).
Renin‑angiotensin system blockade (ACE‑I or ARB) to reduce proteinuria.
Calcineurin inhibitors (cyclosporine or tacrolimus) for persistent proteinuria when ACE‑I/ARB insufficient.
Avoid high‑dose steroids alone; they add little benefit and increase infection risk.
Anticoagulation (low‑molecular‑weight heparin) when albumin <20 g/L and no contraindication.
sections.p: Treat the underlying trigger first, then control proteinuria and protect renal function. Use agents that are affordable and monitor for toxicity.

b: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis – usually steroid‑responsive, shows segmental sclerosis on biopsy.
Minimal change disease – more common in children, responds dramatically to steroids.
Amyloidosis – systemic signs, Congo‑red positive deposits.
sections.p: Other causes of adult nephrotic syndrome can mimic MN clinically.

b: PLA2R antibodies can be negative in early primary MN; biopsy remains gold standard.
Serum albumin may appear normal if fluid shifts are limited; rely on quantitative proteinuria.
sections.p: Certain tests may be falsely negative or normal in early disease.

b: Nephrotic syndrome + positive PLA2R → primary MN.
Nephrotic syndrome + hepatitis B positivity → secondary MN; treat hepatitis first.
Rapid creatinine rise → consider acute tubular necrosis superimposed on MN.
sections.p: Focus on pattern recognition, differential diagnosis, and management hierarchy.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden increase in oedema with shortness of breath
New onset of haematuria or rapid rise in serum creatinine
Signs of deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism
